On Textual Witnesses

In the present edition, nine textual witnesses have been included, six of which represent the work in its entirety, but five of them (i.e., excluding F) contain internal abridgments. In the two manuscripts PV, these abridgments are consequential to the additional text I have identified. In the original, this text had a secondary character as a marginal accompanying text; Posthumously, however, it was granted the status of a separate work with the title 'Book of Composite Medicine', which appears only in secondary literature, while the original text represented by PV

was published as 'Liber simplicis medicinae' with this secondary title (see Embach, pp. 290ff.).

The four other textual witnesses (FWSB), on the other hand, follow the intention of integrating the supplementary text into the original text more or less according to its content-related relationship to the original text – and at the appropriate points. All four textual witnesses exhibit significant differences:

– F integrated the supplementary text most completely and almost always at the logically correct points in the original text.

– W proceeds less completely when incorporating the supplementary text into the original text. Often, the logically correct integration is disregarded, so that the supplementary text is sometimes even inserted nonsensically into the preceding or following chapter. Behmann retains the marginal separation of the additional text.

– The Strasbourg early edition (S) abridges the basic text considerably, but integrates a significant amount of additional text, particularly in the book on plants and the preceding book on metals, sometimes even exceeding that transmitted by F.

– B transmits the basic text with many abridgments and greater stemmatological proximity to PV than the other manuscripts, but unlike PV, it also integrates additional text on several occasions. The Hildegard text is also interrupted chapter by chapter by shorter text passages from other authors, placed before or after them. These remain unconsidered in the current edition.

– f contains only the 'Liber de lapidibus' (IV), complete except for the last four chapters, extensively and in close textual proximity to F.

The early Strasbourg edition must have been based on a manuscript that, like F and W, is very close to the original or an early copy by Volmar. However, the text underwent a profound redaction in its book division, resulting in the complete omission of Book IV ('De lapidibus') and the combined publication of the remaining books into four: II and IX become I, I becomes II, III remains III, and V–VIII become V. Hildegard's German words were subject to a strong tendency toward Latinization. This may, in part, already be based on Volmar's interlinear Latin alternatives in the original.

The complete regrouping of the chapters in the Book of Plants—as can be seen in the index to Book I—obviously occurred for several reasons:

– The useful plants in fields and gardens were to be grouped together and placed first, in contrast to those growing wild everywhere in nature.

In summary: Sempervivum (houseleek) is hot and dry, healthful when boiled with wine or honey-water to ease liver, lung and chest pain and to clear the mind. A separate note (Semperviva/Hußwurcz) says it is cold and unfit to eat because of its fatty nature; its juice mixed with the milk of a woman ten to twelve weeks past bearing a son, dropped into the ear, restores hearing to the deaf. Bryonia (Schyswurcz) is hot and of no use as food; its heat is dangerous near poison, weakening it if burned nearby, much as wine loses strength when exposed overnight in a gourd. Roasted and cut while hot, its smell harms snakes and bees, and even affects a man unless he has first eaten rue, for it contains humors so troublesome that it can kill men and worms alike. Yet boiled in water and applied hot to ulcerated feet, it draws out putrefaction. Polypodium (steinfarn) is hot and dry; a thin, not-too-weak man with visceral pain should take its powder mixed with a third part of sage to reduce bad humors, since their combined heat and dryness counter excess moisture. A very weak man should instead drink wine boiled with honey together with this powder, whose heat strengthens him while the powder still reduces bad humors; but a healthy, fleshy man should avoid both, lest his good humors be weakened. Vehedistil carries the coldness of dew and is very effective against stings: mixed with a little orechter seluen and reduced to juice in water, it should be drunk immediately after a sting to bring relief. Book VI, Chapter 1 - THE GRIFFIN

The griffin is very hot [in nature], and has something of the nature of a bird and something of the nature of a beast. It is so swift, in the manner of a bird, that if the bulk of its body did not weigh it down, it would fly almost as swiftly as an arrow. But, in the manner of a beast, it eats men. When it flies into the air it does not fly into the burning heat [of the sun], but nevertheless it comes a little near it. Its flesh is not fit for a man to eat, for if a man were to eat of its flesh he would be greatly harmed, since it has neither the full nature of a bird nor the full nature of a beast within itself, but has a defect in both natures.

When the time approaches for her to lay her eggs, she seeks out a hole that is large inside but so narrow and constricted at its mouth that she can scarcely enter it. And within it, because of her fear of the lion, she carefully guards her eggs, for the lion can smell them from afar and, if he can reach them, he tramples and crushes them. Yet the griffin always lies in wait for the lion and does not allow him to remain near her, scorning his strength. She likewise does not allow a bear near her, since he is weaker than the lion. And she lays her eggs in such a way that neither the brightness of the sun nor the breath of the wind can touch them.

But neither her flesh, nor her eggs, nor anything else belonging to her is of much use as medicine, because in her two natures she has more defect than perfection.
